easy.heading: Warming Up With Some Quick Wins
easy.body:
Hey there! I hope you are having a wonderful Monday. I just sat down with my morning brew and tackled today's easy Pips puzzle by Ian Livengood. Right away, I noticed those greater than 5 hints at cells [0,0] and [0,4]. Since we only have a few dominoes with high numbers like the [1,6] and [6,5], I knew those had to go in the corners. I started by placing the [1,6] domino vertically at [1,0] and [0,0]. This worked perfectly because it put the 6 in the spot that needed to be greater than 5.

Once that was in place, the rest of the left side started to make sense. Cell [1,0] was now a 1, and since cells [1,0] and [1,1] had to sum up to 5, I knew cell [1,1] had to be a 4. That led me to use the [4,4] domino for the pair at [1,1] and [2,1]. It is always so satisfying when the first two pieces lock in like that! From there, I saw the equals constraint at [2,1] and [2,2]. Since [2,1] was a 4, [2,2] had to be a 4 too, but wait, looking at my remaining dominoes like [3,3], I had to adjust my path slightly to fit everything into the empty cell constraints.

I finished up by looking at the right side. The empty cell at [1,4] meant I had to be careful with how I placed the [6,5] domino. I ended up putting it at [0,4] and [1,4] which satisfied the greater than 5 rule for that top corner. The equals region at [1,2] and [1,3] was the final piece of the puzzle, using the [3,3] domino to wrap things up. It was a nice, gentle start to the week that really got my brain moving without being too stressful.

medium.heading: Finding My Rhythm In The Middle Ground
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today felt like a step up in logic, especially with that big sum of 8 region in the middle. I started by looking for the most restrictive spots. The cell at [3,4] has a less than 1 constraint, which is basically a fancy way of saying it has to be 0! Since I had a [0,1] domino in my set, I placed it at [3,4] and [2,4]. This immediately cleared up that bottom right corner and gave me a starting point to branch out from.

Next, I focused on the sum of 11 at [1,2] and [1,3]. To get to 11 with two numbers, you almost always need a 5 and a 6. I looked at my dominoes and saw the [5,6] piece. Placing that there helped me visualize the rest of the board. The equals constraint at [0,0] and [1,0] was also a huge help. I used the [0,0] domino there, which felt right because it kept the higher numbers available for the areas that needed big sums, like the greater than 11 spot at the bottom.

Speaking of that bottom section, cells [3,0] and [3,1] needed to be greater than 11. In a standard domino set where the highest number is 6, the only way to get a sum higher than 11 is to have two 6s or a 6 and a 5. I spent a little time juggling the [4,6] and [4,2] dominoes to see where they fit. Once I realized the [4,6] domino could bridge the gap to the sum of 8 region, everything fell into place. It took a bit of trial and error to make sure the equals region at [0,2] and [0,3] didn't use up a number I needed elsewhere, but I got there in the end!

hard.heading: Tackling The Kurchan Conundrum
hard.body:
Wow, Rodolfo Kurchan really brought his A-game for this hard puzzle! The grid looked a bit intimidating at first with all those overlapping sum and equals constraints. The breakthrough for me was the triple equals constraint involving cells [1,2], [2,1], and [2,2]. It is rare to see three cells linked like that. I had to look for dominoes that had matching numbers. I eventually used the [2,2] domino for [1,2] and [2,2], which then forced [2,1] to be a 2 as well.

Another tricky area was the bottom where [3,4] and [4,4] had to sum to more than 10. That is a very high target! I knew I needed my biggest dominoes there, so I saved the [6,6] and [5,5] pieces for that section. Placing the [6,6] domino at [3,4] and [4,4] was a game-changer. It meant those cells contributed 12 to the total, easily clearing the target. This also helped me figure out where the [5,4] and [4,3] dominoes should go to satisfy the greater than 4 and greater than 3 constraints nearby.

The final challenge was the top row. We had sums of 10 and 4 and 3 all crowded together. The sum of 10 at [0,1] and [0,2] had to be a 6 and a 4 or a 5 and a 5. Since I had already used some high numbers, I had to be very careful. I ended up using the [6,5] domino for that area, which left me with just enough room to fit the [0,4] and [0,3] dominoes into their respective sum regions. This puzzle was like a high-stakes game of Tetris where every move could ruin the whole thing, but man, it felt good to see that success message pop up!

explanation.tips: When you start a Pips puzzle, always look for the greater than or less than constraints first because they usually limit your choices to just one or two dominoes. I also find it helpful to look for equals regions that span across two different dominoes, as this forces those two pieces to share a specific number. Don't be afraid to leave a section and come back to it if you get stuck; sometimes filling in the other side of the board makes the tricky part obvious.
explanation.learned:
Today I learned how constructor Ian Livengood uses empty cells to act as walls that funnel your dominoes into specific orientations. It makes the easy and medium puzzles feel very structured. I also realized that in the hard puzzles by Rodolfo Kurchan, the sum targets like greater than 10 are actually your best friends because they narrow down your pool of dominoes so significantly.

I also noticed a recurring pattern where placing a double domino, like a [4,4] or [2,2], often helps solve those tricky equals constraints because it provides the same number for two adjacent cells in a single move. It is a handy little trick to keep in mind for future puzzles!

faqs.question: How do you play the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: You play by placing a set of dominoes onto a grid so that they satisfy various constraints like sums, equal values, or greater than/less than targets. Each domino can only be used once, and every cell must be filled unless it is marked as an empty region.

faqs.question: What does an equals sign mean in a Pips puzzle region?
faqs.answer: An equals sign means that all the cells within that specific colored region must have the exact same number. If the region covers two different dominoes, the parts of those dominoes inside the region must match.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed diagonally in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: No, dominoes must be placed either horizontally or vertically across two adjacent cells. They cannot be placed diagonally.

faqs.question: What is a sum target in a Pips region?
faqs.answer: A sum target is a number inside a region that indicates what all the pips in those cells must add up to. For example, if a region of two cells has a target of 10, the numbers in those two cells must add up to exactly 10.

faqs.question: How many dominoes are used in a standard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: The number of dominoes varies depending on the puzzle size and difficulty. Easy puzzles usually have around 5 dominoes, while hard puzzles can have 12 or more.

faqs.question: Are the numbers on the dominoes always 0 through 6?
faqs.answer: Most Pips puzzles use a standard double-six domino set, meaning the numbers on each half of a domino range from 0 to 6. Always check the provided domino list for the day to be sure!
